Trying to Conceive

Why periods happen: and what your cycle can tell you

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A period is part of the hormonal cycle that can prepare the body for pregnancy. When pregnancy does not occur, changes in hormone levels lead the lining of the uterus to shed. Menstruation is common, but disabling pain or bleeding that disrupts daily life is not something you simply have to accept.

What happens during the cycle

Hormonal signals involving the brain and ovaries help coordinate the menstrual cycle. The uterine lining develops, and in an ovulatory cycle an egg is released from an ovary.

After ovulation, progesterone helps support the lining. If pregnancy does not develop, estrogen and progesterone levels fall, and part of the lining leaves the body through the cervix and vagina. Menstrual fluid contains blood as well as tissue and other fluid.

Bleeding alone does not prove that ovulation occurred normally. Bleeding associated with hormonal contraception, for example, may follow a different pattern from a natural ovulatory cycle.

The hypothalamus and pituitary in the brain send signals to the ovaries, which then affect the uterine lining. Ovulation, fertilisation and implantation are distinct steps: sperm fertilises an egg, and a resulting embryo may later implant in the lining. When the hormonal support for the lining falls without an ongoing pregnancy, bleeding begins and the cycle can start again.

Count from one starting day to the next

Cycle length is measured from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. It is not the interval from the end of bleeding to the next start.

A 28-day cycle is an average, not a requirement. Cycle length and the number of bleeding days vary between people and across life stages. Early teenage cycles, breastfeeding, perimenopause and hormonal contraception can change the pattern.

Record the start and end of bleeding and any symptoms that matter to you. A persistent change from your usual pattern may be more informative than comparing yourself with another person. An app’s predicted date is an estimate, not proof of when ovulation happens.

Periods commonly begin in the early teens, but the age varies; a first period by age 15 is an assessment threshold rather than a requirement to start between 11 and 14. Menopause most often occurs between 45 and 55, with an average around 51 in the UK. These are population patterns, not deadlines for every person.

How much blood is typical?

A commonly quoted average is roughly two to three tablespoons of blood over the whole period: not each day. The total fluid you see is not all blood, and the appearance of a pad, tampon or toilet bowl cannot measure it precisely.

You do not need to calculate an exact volume before asking for help. Bleeding that requires very frequent changes, leaks through clothes or bedding, lasts more than seven days or limits ordinary activities is worth discussing with a clinician.

Heavy bleeding can lead to iron-deficiency anaemia. Unusual tiredness, breathlessness or reduced exercise tolerance should be mentioned as well. The impact on your life matters, even if you cannot describe the amount in millilitres.

Pain deserves attention too

Mild cramps can accompany the uterus contracting, but pain that repeatedly stops you sleeping, going to school or working deserves assessment. Conditions such as endometriosis, adenomyosis or fibroids may be involved, although symptoms alone cannot establish a diagnosis.

Heat and appropriate pain relief may help. Ask a pharmacist or clinician which medicine is suitable if pregnancy is possible, you have another medical condition or you take other medicines. Seek urgent advice if the pain is severe or worse than usual and usual measures are not helping.

Periods can be reduced or sometimes stopped with treatment

You can discuss menstrual suppression if you want fewer bleeding days or relief from heavy or painful periods. Options include certain hormonal pills, patches or rings used in an extended pattern, progestin-only methods, injections and a hormonal intrauterine system.

Some people stop bleeding with a chosen method; others have lighter or less frequent bleeding, and spotting can occur. There is no single success percentage for every pill, implant or hormonal intrauterine device. The formulation, dose, duration and individual response matter.

A monthly withdrawal bleed is not required for health when using an appropriate hormonal regimen. The lining does not need a monthly “clean-out.” However, the best method depends on your health history, preferences and pregnancy plans, and some menstrual treatments are not contraceptives.

The contraceptive injection can delay the return of fertility after it is stopped; this is not the same as permanent infertility. If you hope to conceive soon, discuss the timing before choosing a method. Do not change a prescribed regimen without checking its instructions.

A missed period is not always a disorder

Pregnancy, breastfeeding, menopause, hormonal medicines, stress and changes in energy intake or exercise can affect bleeding. A missed period can also have a medical cause.

If pregnancy is possible, take a pregnancy test at the appropriate time. Arrange review for repeatedly missed periods, a substantial unexplained change, or other symptoms such as unusual hair growth or marked weight change. A lack of bleeding while using contraception does not by itself prove that pregnancy is impossible.

A period is not a test of femininity, health or fertility on its own. Some healthy people do not menstruate because of treatment or their life stage, and some people with regular bleeding still need help with symptoms or conception.

When to seek urgent help

Get urgent medical advice for rapidly heavy bleeding. Call emergency services if heavy bleeding is accompanied by fainting, severe weakness, chest pain or difficulty breathing. Do not wait to measure the total blood loss.

If pregnancy is possible, bleeding with severe or one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain or faintness needs urgent assessment for causes including ectopic pregnancy. Bleeding after menopause also needs review, even if it is light.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS advises assessment when pain, heavy bleeding or persistent cycle changes affect daily life.

Clinical menstrual-suppression guidance supports individualized hormonal options, realistic expectations and discussion of future pregnancy timing.

How BeMama can help

Track the first day, duration and impact of bleeding and bring your goals for lighter or less frequent periods to a care appointment.

When to seek help

Heavy bleeding with faintness, chest pain or breathing difficulty, or possible pregnancy with severe pain, requires urgent care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next.
  • The usual blood-loss estimate refers to the whole period, not each day.
  • Pain and bleeding that disrupt life deserve care.
  • Suitable hormonal treatment can reduce or stop bleeding, but results vary.

Frequently asked questions

Does everyone need a 28-day cycle?

No. Cycle lengths vary. Track your own pattern and ask about persistent or unexplained changes.

Is it unhealthy to skip the monthly bleed on hormonal contraception?

A monthly withdrawal bleed is not medically necessary with a suitable regimen. Check which schedule is appropriate for the specific product and your health history.

Does having a period guarantee that I can get pregnant?

No. Bleeding alone does not establish normal ovulation or evaluate every factor involved in fertility.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
